title: Skewers: the king moves, the piece behind falls
outcomes: Finds a skewer when told to look for one
Checks that the front piece cannot capture the attacker
Checks that nothing can step between, and that taking the piece behind gains material
Tells a skewer from a pin by the order of values on the line
Builds a skewer with a check and guards against one
Says when a check lines up nothing

steps.caption: Black to move. Look at the white king on d3, the knight on f1 and the black bishop on b3. Decide what you would play, and why, before you read on.

claims.statement: Bc4+ is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.prompt: Pick a move and give one reason. The lesson returns to this position, so write what you actually think.

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Spot a skewer in a position nobody has labelled. Test it with four questions: can the front piece take the attacker, can something step in, is the piece behind guarded, can the front piece answer with a threat? Build one with a forcing move. Guard against one in your own games. And say plainly when a check lines up nothing.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white king and the white rook both stand on the first rank, the king in front. The rook on h8 has an open file. Step through.

line.say: The rook checks along the first rank. The white king stands between it and the rook on a1.
The king must leave the rank. It cannot take the rook, which is far away.
Nothing stands between the two rooks now, so the black rook takes the white one.

claims.statement: Rh1+ followed by Rxa1 wins the white rook.

steps.caption: Back to the hook. Step through to see what the bishop was aiming at.

line.say: The bishop checks. The king is on the diagonal, and the knight on f1 stands behind it.
The king steps off the diagonal. Stepping along it would still be check.
Nothing guards the knight, so the bishop takes it.

claims.statement: Bc4+ followed by Bxf1 wins the knight.

steps.text: **Back to your guess.** Look at what you wrote before. If you chose the bishop check, can you now say why the king cannot take the bishop and why the knight is lost? If you chose something else, what did you see that the check misses? Keep your answer, because the later boards test it.

A **skewer** attacks a valuable piece with a second piece lined up behind it. If the front piece is the king, it must move, so the piece behind is lost. If the front piece is a queen or rook, the owner can move it, but only by giving up the piece behind or paying something else. In a pin the order is usually reversed: the cheaper piece stands in front. Most boards so far begin with a check; a quiet one comes later.

steps.caption: White to move. Lichess puzzle record (CC0), from a real game. The black king on e7 and the black queen on d8 lie on one diagonal.

line.say: The bishop checks along the diagonal. The queen stands behind the king.
The king's only safe square is e8; Kd7 would allow mate.
The bishop takes the queen.

claims.statement: Bg5+ followed by Bxd8 wins the queen.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's king and queen already share the e-file, but White's queen cannot check along it yet. From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0), taken from a real game.

line.say: The queen checks, guarded by the pawn on g6. This check is a preparation: the king has only one square, e5, and the queen now reaches the e-file.
Forced: the only legal reply.
Now the check runs down the file, with the black queen behind the king.
The king must leave the file.
The white queen takes the black queen.

claims.statement: Qf7+ followed by Qxe2 wins the black queen.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white king stands on e4 with a white rook on e1 behind it, on the same file.

line.say: The rook checks down the file.
The king steps off the file.
The rook takes the rook that stood behind the king.

claims.statement: Re7+ followed by Rxe1 wins at least four points.

steps.caption: Black to move. The target can be far from the king: the rook on h7 sits at the other end of the diagonal. From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0).

line.say: The bishop checks. The long diagonal runs through the king to the far corner.
The king steps off the diagonal.
The bishop takes the rook at the end of the diagonal.

claims.statement: Bc2+ followed by Bxh7 wins the rook.

steps.caption: White to move. The black king on d4 and its rook on a4 are far apart on the fourth rank. From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0).

line.say: The rook checks along the fourth rank, guarded by the king on g4.
The king steps off the rank.
The rook runs along the rank and takes the black rook.

claims.statement: Rf4+ followed by Rxa4 wins the rook.

steps.text: **Why it works, part one: a king in front.** A check must be answered, and the king cannot stay on the line, so its step is forced. That forced step is the whole trick: the owner has no spare move to rescue the piece behind, because the turn is used up answering the check. A king in front is the strongest case.
steps.chapter: Why it works and when it fails

steps.text: **Part two: a queen or rook in front.** Nothing forces the owner here, so the owner picks the cheaper loss. Count it: a bishop attacks a queen with a rook behind it. The queen steps away and you take the rook, five points for the price of one move. The owner never gives up the queen to save the rook. [I] That is why the front piece should be worth more than what stands behind it.

steps.caption: The same line, reversed order: the knight stands in front of the king, so it is pinned. White to move. White has exactly one good reply, Ke2, which defends the knight, and Black's bishop earns at most a trade.

line.say: The king steps up behind the knight and defends it.
The bishop takes the knight.
The king takes back. An even trade: nothing is won.

claims.statement: The knight on d3 has no legal move: it is pinned to the king.
The engine rates the position as roughly level (depth 16).
After the king steps to e2, it defends the knight.

steps.text: **Part three: swap the order.** Put the cheaper piece in front and the same line becomes a pin or nothing: the owner defends the cheap piece or lets it go and loses only that. So the order of values, not the line itself, decides whether material is won. [H] Skewers may turn up more in endings, where kings are exposed and few pieces can block. We have not tested this.

**Four ways out.** Before you play a skewer, ask what the defender can do. One: take the attacker. Two: step in between, cutting the line. Three: guard the piece behind, so that taking it is only a trade. Four: move the front piece with a threat of its own. [I] These four cover most of what goes wrong. If none of them works and you have checked for a stronger reply, the skewer very likely wins. Keep a place for a fifth: a forcing reply you did not list.

steps.caption: The hook position again, but Black's pawn is no longer on b5. Black to move. Does the check still win the knight?

line.say: The bishop checks, but nothing guards it now.
The king simply takes the bishop.

claims.statement: Bc4+ Kxc4 loses the bishop.
After the check the bishop on c4 is attacked and undefended.

steps.caption: Another change: a white rook on a1 now guards the knight along the first rank. Black to move. Step through.

line.say: The bishop checks as before.
The king steps off the diagonal.
The bishop takes the knight.
The rook takes the bishop. A bishop for a knight: nothing won.

claims.statement: Bc4+ followed by Bxf1 Rxf1 wins no material.
After the king steps away, the rook on a1 is the one piece guarding f1.

steps.caption: The first rook skewer again, with a white bishop on d3 added. Black to move. The bishop can reach f1, between the rook and the king.

line.say: The rook checks, as before.
The bishop steps between the rook and the king. The line is cut.

claims.statement: Rh1+ Bf1 no longer wins the rook (at most one point).
The king guards the bishop on f1, so taking it would lose the rook.

steps.caption: White to move. A bishop can attack the black queen on e5, with the rook on b8 behind it on the same diagonal. The white queen on f3 will guard the bishop. From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0).

line.say: The bishop attacks the queen. The queen on f3 defends it, so the black queen cannot take.
The queen steps off the diagonal and attacks the bishop on f4.
White ignores the threat and takes the rook. The bishop has left f4, so the f-file is open and Black can trade queens.
Black takes the white queen.
White takes back. White is still a rook ahead.

claims.statement: Bf4 followed by Bxb8 wins the rook even after the queen trade.
After Bf4 the queen on f3 guards the bishop.

steps.text: **Where skewers come from.** Sometimes both pieces already stand on one line and you need only a safe attack on the front one. Otherwise you build the line: a check drives the king to a square where something stands behind it. [H] Skewers that need a preparing check may be common in practice; we have not counted them. A check from a distance cannot be answered by taking the checker, which is why queens and rooks suit it. A checker next to the king works if something defends it.
steps.chapter: Set it up, or stop it

steps.caption: Black to move. White's king and rook are not on one line yet, and the bishop on c7 is aimed at h2. From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0).

line.say: The queen checks. The bishop on c7 guards h2, so the king cannot take.
The king has only one square: it steps onto the first rank, in front of its own rook.
A second check along the first rank. Now the rook on a1 is behind the king.
The king runs.
The queen takes the rook.

claims.statement: Qh2+ followed by Qh1+ and Qxa1 wins the rook.
After Qh2+ the bishop on c7 guards the queen.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's queen stands on f1. The black king is on e5. Can a check push the king onto a line with the queen? From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0).

line.say: The queen checks along the diagonal.
The king steps to f4, onto the f-file.
A second check. The black queen on f1 is now behind the king on the same file.
The king takes the pawn on g4 and leaves the file.
The queen takes the black queen.

claims.statement: Qc3+ followed by Qf6+ and Qxf1 wins the black queen.

steps.caption: White to move. The black king on c7 and the black rook on d8 lie on one diagonal. After that, a second line may open. From a Lichess puzzle record (CC0).

line.say: The bishop checks. The rook on d8 stands behind the king.
The king steps to the eighth rank.
A rook check along the eighth rank. The rook on d8 is behind the king again.
The king steps off the rank.
The rook takes the rook. The queen on e7 could take back, but the bishop on a5 guards d8, so White still comes out a rook ahead. Black keeps a queen, so the game goes on.

claims.statement: Ba5+ followed by Ra8+ and Rxd8 wins at least five points.
Before Rxd8, two white pieces attack d8: the rook on a8 and the bishop on a5, so a recapture by the queen loses.

steps.text: **Stopping one before it lands.** Four cures. Move the front piece off the line. Move the piece behind off it. Guard the piece behind, so that taking it only trades. Keep something ready to block. [I] Moving the king is often simplest, because a check can drive it, but in the next position the engine slightly prefers moving the knight (depth 16, close).

steps.caption: White to move. Before choosing a move, ask what Black threatens. The h-file is open, and White's king and rook share the first rank.

claims.statement: If White passed, Rh1+ would win the white rook.

steps.caption: White has stepped the king off the first rank. Black to move. The same rook check is no longer a skewer.

line.say: The rook goes to h1, where the rook on a1 now looks at it along the rank.
The white rook takes the black rook.

claims.statement: Rh1 now loses the rook.

steps.caption: A second cure from the same start: White moved the rook off the first rank instead. Black to move.

line.say: The rook checks, but nothing stands behind the king.
The king steps away. Black has won nothing.

claims.statement: Rh1+ wins no material here.

steps.caption: The position of that item. Black to move. Black can move the piece behind the king off the diagonal, or the king itself.

line.say: The knight steps off the diagonal. A bishop check on c5 would now line up nothing.
White's bishop must retreat, because the knight attacks it; for example to e3. The skewer is gone.

claims.statement: Nd7 and Ke6 both hold the position; Nd7 is slightly preferred (depth 16).

steps.text: **What coaches say.** Dan Heisman teaches listing the opponent's forcing replies (checks, captures, threats) before each move [S], and treating the opponent as someone who will find the best one [S]. Jeremy Silman puts a look for tactics ahead of positional analysis [S]. [H] One extra question may catch skewers sooner: do my king and another valuable piece share a line? [H] Beginners may see pins before skewers because a pin is easier to picture. Untested; your games are the test.

steps.prompt: Do you agree that one extra question before each move is worth the time? Think of a game you lost to a check that won a piece.

steps.text: **Look-alikes.** A **fork** attacks two pieces from one square. A **pin** has the cheaper piece in front. A **discovered attack** moves one piece to unmask another. A skewer needs a line with the *more valuable* piece in front and something worth taking behind. If the line is blocked, or nothing is behind, the check is only a check.

steps.title: The skewering piece can be taken
steps.prompt: Only the white rook has moved: from d1 to g1.

steps.title: One change each: a block, then nothing behind
steps.prompt: Predict first. In the second position a black bishop stands on d6. In the third, the black rook is not on a8.

steps.text: **Now nobody says skewer.** The next positions are mixed. Some contain a skewer, some only look like one. Run your four questions on every check you consider, and answer no tactic when it is so. If the app asks how sure you are, answer it: it is optional, but it shows you how well you can tell.

**What our own data shows.** Our shipped puzzle set has 47 Lichess-derived positions tagged skewer [V, recounted 7 Nov 2026, counts as of this build]. In 31 the first move is a check. The first move is made by a rook in 22, a bishop in 12, a queen in 8, a king in 2, a knight in 2 and a pawn in 1. [I] Rooks and bishops lead probably because they move along the lines a skewer needs. Small sample, one site.

line.say: The queen checks, guarded by the rook on h8, so the king cannot take.
The king steps off the diagonal.
The queen crosses the whole board and takes the black queen.

claims.statement: Qh7+ followed by Qxb1 wins the black queen.
After Qh7+ the rook on h8 guards the queen.

steps.caption: White to move. Another Lichess puzzle record (CC0). The black king stands on c6, the black queen on f3. Look for the line that joins them.

line.say: The queen checks along the long diagonal, from the far corner.
The king steps off the diagonal.
The queen travels the whole diagonal and takes the black queen.

claims.statement: Qa8+ followed by Qxf3 wins the black queen.

line.say: The bishop checks. The bishop on e8 is behind the king.
The king steps off the diagonal.
The bishop takes the bishop.

steps.prompt: Pick one board from this chapter. What had the side that lost a piece done wrong one move earlier, and what simple move would have avoided it? Say it as a rule for your own play.

steps.text: **Recap.** A skewer attacks the more valuable piece first, with something behind it on the same line. Check four answers: take the attacker, block, guard the piece behind, or move with a threat. Build skewers with checks that push the king onto a line. Guard against them by keeping valuable pieces off shared lines. Many checks line nothing up: say no tactic when that is so.

**Self-check before you write.** Did I say what makes it a skewer and not a pin? Did I say when it fails, using the four answers? Did I describe a position a beginner could set up with a handful of pieces? Did I name one mistake, such as checking when the king can take the attacker? Nothing here is graded; the list is for you.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Explain the skewer to a beginner who knows how the pieces move. Use your own words.
